Physics: All forty keys check out numerically, and the spread across mechanics, electricity, optics and modern physics is well balanced with no essentially duplicated items. The level is appropriate for BITSAT: a healthy base of one-step items (8, 22, 27, 28, 31) offset by genuinely multi-step ones (19, 25, 33, 34), though 19 and 37 sit near the 90-second ceiling. Only q35 needs a clarifying clause about the rope hanging symmetrically before printing.

[minor] The rope's distribution over the pulley is unspecified, so the system's acceleration (and hence key B) is only valid if equal lengths of rope hang on the two sides — add that clause explicitly.

Chemistry: Coverage is broad and reasonably balanced across physical, inorganic and organic chemistry, with most numerical items (52, 60, 66, 74, 78) well-posed, internally consistent and correctly keyed. However, the section leans heavily on trend/ordering items (42, 44, 46, 54, 55, 69, 73, 79), contains two redundant pairs (47/62 and 49/75), and includes one clearly out-of-syllabus Landé-factor question. Fix the contested SN1 ordering and replace the duplicates; Q41 and Q56 are acceptable but sit at the upper edge of the 90-second budget.

[major] The placement of benzyl chloride above the tertiary halide is not defensible: solvolysis data in aqueous/protic media put 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane (3°, ionises readily at RT) ahead of benzyl chloride, so option D is at least as defensible as the keyed A.
[major] This duplicates Q47, which already tests the lone-pair count and shape of XeF4 (2 lone pairs, square planar) by the same VSEPR reasoning; replace it with a different p-block topic.

[major] Landé g-factor/Hund's-rule free-ion moments are outside the BITSAT level (spin-only √n(n+2) is the syllabus formula), and discriminating 10.61 from 10.65 μB needs two full J, L, S computations, far beyond 90 s; the stem also asks "which ion" while the options give only numbers.
[minor] The ">" signs are meant as "earlier than" but read as a magnitude comparison (and clash with the "<" convention used elsewhere in the section); state the sequence with arrows or words.
[major] This retests Q49's content — the low-spin d6 [Fe(CN)6]4− with 0 unpaired electrons versus a weak-field high-spin d6 ion with 4 — so one of the two items must be replaced.

English Proficiency: Coverage is broadly right for BITSAT English Proficiency — synonyms/antonyms, grammar and sentence improvement, two jumbles, an idiom and a well-written reading-comprehension pair — and the Neptune and heat-map jumbles and the RC passage are pitched at an appropriate level. Difficulty is uneven, though: 'brave' and the passive-voice conversion sit far below the rest, while two vocabulary items and the two RC keys test overlapping content, wasting slots in a 15-item section. Repairing the split-clause jumble, replacing the duplicated vocabulary item and raising the floor on the easiest questions would make this section print-ready.

[major] P and Q are two halves of a single sentence (P ends in a comma and Q begins with lowercase "but"), so the four labelled units plus the fixed first and last sentences cannot form the stated "five-sentence paragraph", and the P–Q link is given away rather than tested.

[major] This item duplicates Q84 almost exactly — both reward the idea of "carefully checking dates and sources/references" (meticulous / painstaking) — so one of the two must be replaced with a different vocabulary point.
[major] "Brave → courageous" with timid/careful/weary as distractors is far below BITSAT level and merely repeats Q81's synonym task at trivial difficulty; a genuinely tested word is needed.

[minor] The key ("figures alone cannot establish whether the most heat-exposed residents gained shade") simply restates Q94's central-idea key, so the two comprehension items are not independent and one should probe a different detail or inference.

Logical Reasoning: The section covers a reasonable spread of BITSAT logical-reasoning types (series, syllogism, blood relations, classification, coding, cubes) at broadly the right 60–90 second difficulty, and the keys for the verifiable text items are correct. Its main weaknesses are production-related — q97 has no figures at all — and a redundancy between the two letter-shift items q104 and q105. Add the missing artwork, reword q96's stem, and swap one coding item for a different sub-skill before printing.

[minor] All six listed strings are meaningful English words, so the stem should ask how many "can be formed from the letters of counterintelligence" rather than how many "are meaningful four-letter English words", otherwise option D (Six) is literally defensible.
[major] The four option figures are entirely blank, so the odd-figure-out item has no content and cannot be answered or keyed.

[major] This duplicates q104, since both items are solved by the same alphabet letter-shift coding skill; replace one with a genuinely different coding type (e.g., number/substitution or conditional coding).

Mathematics: Every key in the section checks out numerically, and the coverage of algebra, calculus, vectors/3D and coordinate geometry is broadly sound, though integral calculus (five items) and sets/functions counting (four) are over-weighted while trigonometry, sequences and binomial theorem are barely represented. The level is mostly appropriate, but q106 is off-syllabus, q134 and q146 sit at the very top of the 90-second budget, and q111/q113/q137 are close to formula recall. Removing one of the two onto-function counts and one of the duplicate substitution integrals, and retagging q141, would sharpen both balance and discrimination.

[major] The 4xy term makes this a rotated ellipse whose eccentricity can only be found by rotating axes / diagonalising the quadratic form, which is outside the BITSAT standard-form conics syllabus and far beyond a 90-second solve (the options also carry doubled brackets, e.g. "((1,-2),...)" ).

[minor] ∫xe^x dx is a memorised textbook result and the stem even names the method ("by parts"), so the item tests recall only; drop the method hint or use a genuine by-parts integrand such as x ln x or x sin x.

[major] This repeats the inclusion–exclusion surjection count already tested in q114 and needs two such counts (8400/4 and 1560/4), making it both redundant and over-long for the time budget; replace it with a different counting idea.
[minor] It uses exactly the same one-step "numerator is the derivative of the denominator" substitution as q113, so one of the two should be swapped for a different integration technique.
[minor] The item is tagged Statistics but is pure coordinate geometry (reflection of a point in a line), which misrepresents the blueprint and leaves statistics with only one genuine item.

Physics: All forty keys check out numerically and there are no duplicate concepts or figure/data inconsistencies, so the section is usable essentially as it stands. Coverage is well spread across mechanics, electricity, optics and modern physics, but roughly a third of the items (2, 7, 8, 22, 27, 28, 31) are single-substitution recall while a small cluster (11, 19, 25, 34, 35) sits at the upper edge of the 90-second budget. Only wording polish on 20 and 30 and the off-syllabus rotating-liquid item 36 need attention before printing.

[minor] Reword the stem as "the fourth-order bright fringe on A's side" — "the bright fringe that was fourth on A's side before insertion" is convoluted and invites students to read it as a fixed point on the screen (12 mm) rather than a fixed fringe order (18 mm).

[minor] "The neutral atomic masses of a parent nucleus, its daughter nucleus and a helium atom" is self-contradictory (a nucleus has no electrons); say "the neutral atomic masses of the parent atom, the daughter atom and helium", which is what the electron-balanced Q-value calculation actually uses.

[minor] Rigid-body rotation of a liquid (paraboloidal free surface, centre depth h₀ − ω²R²/4g) sits outside the NCERT/BITSAT fluids syllabus and needs a result students must recall rather than derive in 90 s; replace with a standard hydrostatics/Bernoulli item.

Chemistry: The section is well spread across physical, inorganic and organic chemistry, and almost all keys and distractors check out arithmetically (q52, q56, q60, q66, q74 are cleanly constructed with self-consistent data). The main weaknesses are redundancy — two VSEPR items on XeF4 and two crystal-field items on [Fe(CN)6]4− — plus one genuinely ambiguous SN1 ordering and one Landé-factor question that is well beyond BITSAT level and time. Trimming q41's computation and replacing the duplicated and out-of-syllabus items would leave a paper of appropriate, mostly moderate difficulty.

[minor] The item chains a full bond-enthalpy combustion calculation (11 bond terms) to a Hess's-law step and then the ΔH→ΔU conversion, making it a ~2-minute question; supplying ΔH_c(C2H4) or removing one stage would bring it within the 90 s budget (key −117.6 kJ mol⁻¹ is otherwise correct).

[major] The benzyl-versus-tertiary SN1 ranking is genuinely contested — actual solvolysis rates make 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane faster than benzyl chloride, so option D is as defensible as the keyed A.
[major] This duplicates q47, which already tests exactly the same VSEPR fact (XeF4: two lone pairs, square planar) alongside ClF3 and SF4.

[major] Hund's-rule/Landé g_J free-ion moments are outside the BITSAT syllabus (which uses spin-only moments), and separating Ho³⁺ (10.61) from Dy³⁺ (10.65) requires four-significant-figure work on three ions, far beyond 90 s; the stem also asks "which ion" while the options give only numbers.
[major] This repeats q49's strong-field/weak-field spin-state reasoning with the same complex [Fe(CN)6]4− giving low-spin, 0 unpaired electrons, so the two items test essentially the same skill.

English Proficiency: The section covers the expected BITSAT spread — synonyms/antonyms, vocabulary in context, grammar (agreement, tense, preposition, voice), idiom, two jumbles and a paired RC set — and the keys are correct throughout, with the RC passage and its inference question the strongest items. Level is on the easy side: qnos 84, 88 and 92 are single-step recall with weak distractors, and the meticulous/painstaking overlap wastes a slot that could carry a harder discrimination item. Fixing the P–Q punctuation in qno 82 and replacing one of the duplicated vocabulary items would make the section print-ready.

[minor] P ends with a comma and Q begins with lowercase "but", so they are two halves of one sentence rather than the separate sentences the "five-sentence paragraph" stem promises, and this punctuation hand-holds the P–Q link; make P and Q self-contained sentences (e.g. P ends with a full stop, Q begins "However, two mathematicians...").

[major] This item duplicates qno 84 almost exactly — both keys turn on the same "careful/thorough" word (painstaking ≈ meticulous) in the identical context of checking dates and sources — so one of the two must be replaced with a different vocabulary target.
[minor] The stem's "the word given in capital" is unidiomatic; use "the word given in capitals" (or "in capital letters").

Logical Reasoning: Apart from the figure-based items, the section covers a reasonable spread of BITSAT logical-reasoning types (word formation, series, syllogism, classification, blood relations, cubes, coding) and all verifiable keys are correct. The level is on the easy side — most items are single-step and solvable in well under 90 s — and the two letter-shift items (104, 105) make the coding weight redundant. Fixing the missing figure in Q97 and swapping one coding item for a slightly more demanding puzzle would give a better-balanced section.
[major] The item asks for the odd figure out but all four options are empty and no figure is supplied, so the question is unanswerable as printed.

[major] This duplicates Q104 almost exactly in skill (both are simple alphabet-shift transformations of a four-letter word), so one of the two should be replaced by a genuinely different reasoning type (e.g., a non-verbal or arrangement item).

Mathematics: Coverage is well spread across algebra, calculus, coordinate geometry, vectors and probability, and almost all keys check out (107, 110, 118, 127, 132, 139, 143, 144 are all sound and appropriately pitched). The section needs one key correction (146), removal of the rotated-conic item 106 as off-syllabus, a topic-tag fix at 141, and de-duplication of the two onto-function counts (114/134). Difficulty is slightly light at the bottom end — 111, 137, 149 and 150 are one-step recall — while 128, 130 and 144 sit at the upper time limit, so swapping one trivial item for a mid-level one would improve balance.

[major] The ellipse carries an xy term, so its centre/eccentricity need rotation of axes (eigenvalues of [[5,2],[2,2]]), which is outside the BITSAT conics syllabus and far beyond 90 s; options A, C and D also print a stray doubled bracket "$((1,-2)$".
[major] This duplicates qno 114 — both are inclusion–exclusion counts of onto functions between finite sets — so one of the pair should be replaced by a different functions/relations item.
[minor] The item is tagged "Statistics" but is straight-line coordinate geometry (reflection of a point in a line); the tag should read Coordinate Geometry (the key A is correct).
[major] The key is wrong: with t = 2x−1 the odd part vanishes and I = ½∫₀¹ dt/((1+t²)√(2−t²)) = ½·(1/√3)arctan(√3 tan θ)|₀^{π/4} = π/(6√3) ≈ 0.302, i.e. option C, not B.
